How we turned Mount Everest into a dump

It's a shame what has happened to Mount Everest. Unfortunately it is only going to get worse as more and more people try to climb the mountain each year. I was stunned how many of the climbers don't follow LNT (Leave No Trace), a very common ethos in the hiking/camping communities. If people are unable to carry their own trash, they should not be allowed to reach the summit

Most of the people on these things are very rich, they don't want to be bothered with LNT, they've never been on a mountain before let alone knowing simple rules like that. If the Sherpas stopped taking people who didn't respect the mountain it would cut big time into their jobs, and likely they would get backlash from angry rich people causing problems for them.

It's a horrible situation right now but it'll only get worse as the government there makes the paths easier and easier until you don't really need a Sherpa because of the stairs and markers and paths cut into the rock. It'll get to the point that it'll be safe enough not to be a risk at all and then it'll open the flood gates to people who really can't afford it right now because of the need for adventure companies and liability, then the mountain will be truly broken from the hundreds of thousands of yearly visitors.

Don't get me wrong everyone should be able to do whatever they want, but given the local governments lack of care when it comes to preserving it's world famous landmark I doubt they will turn away more customers even if it means destroying it.

I don't know if it's a lack of care so much as a lack of resources. It's a dirt poor country, what exactly are they supposed to do to stop people from doing the one thing that brings outsiders to their country? It's an awkward situation, similar to many poor Caribbean islands dealing with tourists on their beaches. It's an economic reality more than anything else, if your poor, you're willing to trade a lot for a few bucks. If you're rich you have the luxury not to put up with things you don't like.

And my understanding of sherpas is that they're not exactly masters of the mountain, they're just locals doing a dangerous job because there's nothing else to do, and if they didn't do the work other locals would. They're not in a position to turn anybody away.

Everest is just a weird situation. If I were a serious climber, which I'm not, I doubt I'd climb Everest. It's very crowded and very hazardous (nope.jpg), a brutal combination. But it will always have allure, because it is the tallest mountain in the world, so I guess better safe than dead. I'm not sure there's a good answer to all this.

There's no answer for this, the mountain will always attract people and as time goes on it'll become more attractive to tourists as the government and the communities make the area more tourist friendly. They rely on that trade and money input. It's a self serving cycle that'll make poorer people richer and a lot more people will see Everest before they die.

But this will lead to the mountain changing from a wilderness bastion of raw natural power to another holiday destination with nature walks and skiing. And all the ills that come from that transformation will fall upon the mountain and it will never again be what we remember. More of the world will end up like this as time goes on, technologies improve and allow more ease of travel in even the most difficult places of the world, eventually nowhere will be free of human impact and we'll only remember the wild as a distant memory that is shown in paintings and books.
